Our story

Centuries of learning

Drepung Monastery was founded near Lhasa in 1416 by Jamyang Chöje Tashi Palden, a disciple of Je Tsongkhapa. Loseling grew into the largest of its colleges and was closely tied to the Dalai Lamas: the Second Dalai Lama made his residence there in 1494.

Monks at Loseling live and study in khangtsens, or regional houses. Tsangpa Khangtsen began in the eighteenth century with a few dozen monks and grew steadily into the house that carries its name today. The name refers to Tsang, the region of west-central Tibet.

After 1959, Drepung was re-established in exile in Mundgod, Karnataka, and the Khangtsen with it. Today it is one of the 24 khangtsens of Drepung Loseling, with monks mainly from Tibet, India, Nepal and Bhutan.

A khangtsen gives monks a home while they study, so they can become the teachers who carry the Buddha’s words forward.

The journey so far

  1. 1416

    Drepung Monastery is founded near Lhasa.

  2. 1494

    A few dozen monks found what becomes Tsangpa Khangtsen.

  4. After 1959

    Drepung is re-established in exile in Mundgod, Karnataka.

    Drepung Tsangpa Buddhist Cultural Society is registered in Karnataka.

  10. Next

    Painting, utilities and fencing, and the first monks move in.

Our lineage

A lineage of teachers

Masters who trained in Tsangpa Khangtsen include:

  • The successive incarnations of Tutor Yeshe GyaltsenTutor to the 8th Dalai Lama, Jamphel Gyatso
  • The 92nd throne-holder of Ganden
  • The great Khenchen Yeshi Jinpa
  • Geshe Thupten WangyalFormer Abbot of Tsechokling Monastery, Dharamsala
  • Geshe Dorji DamdulDirector of Tibet House, New Delhi, and former English translator to His Holiness the Dalai Lama
  • Geshe Lobsang DawaFormer Dharma teacher at the Institute of Buddhist Dialectics, McLeod Ganj
  • Geshe Thupten Palsang

The Khangtsen today

Study, prayer and community

Our monks range from young novices to senior teachers. The day is shaped by study, debate and prayer, and through the year the courtyard fills with ceremonies, celebrations and guests who come to learn with us.

Study and debate

Monks follow Drepung Loseling’s programme in Buddhist philosophy, logic and debate, the long path toward the Geshe degree.

Prayers and pujas

The community gathers daily in the prayer hall and performs prayers on request, including the 21 Tara prayers, Tara sadhana and Dharmapala rituals.

Study retreats

We organise study retreats for participants from across India and around the world, hosted at the Khangtsen in Mundgod.

Training young monks

Since 2018 we have welcomed boys from Nepal and the Indian Himalayan regions, who receive traditional and modern education.

Celebrations and visitors

We mark major occasions together, such as His Holiness the Dalai Lama’s 90th birthday, and welcome friends and pilgrims who visit Mundgod.

Why we are building

Our home has outgrown itself

For years our prayer hall has been overcrowded and there have not been enough rooms. Some of the current rooms are old and in poor condition. In 2019 we decided to rebuild on a new, larger site, so every monk can live within one compound.

The old site is too small

There is no room for a larger prayer hall or more quarters on the land we occupy today.

The soil can’t take more floors

The ground beneath the existing three-storey blocks can’t support the foundations needed to build higher.

New monks need space

Since 2018, 25 boys from Nepal and the Indian Himalayan regions joined, then five more by October 2024, nine in 2025, with three expected by the end of 2026. Several left because of cramped living space.

Where we are

The walls are rising

Ground was broken in February 2024. Most of the work so far has gone into the monks’ quarters, with the prayer hall partly under way. With funding in place, we expect to finish within a year.
